payload.content:
Overview of the Algorithms domain (no single algorithm yet).

WHAT AN ALGORITHM IS. A step-by-step method that turns an input into an output, precise enough for a machine to follow. The domain asks two questions about every method: (1) is it correct, i.e. does it always give the right answer? (2) is it efficient, i.e. how much time and memory does it need as the input grows?

WORKED EXAMPLE: FINDING A NAME IN 1 BILLION SORTED NAMES. Method A, check every name: up to 1,000,000,000 steps in the worst case. Method B, binary search: open at the middle; if the middle name comes after the target alphabetically, discard the second half, otherwise discard the first; repeat. 1 billion -> 500 million -> 250 million -> ... leaves one name after about 30 halvings. So about 30 steps against 1,000,000,000. Doubling to 2 billion items costs only one more step (31), because the work grows with log n.

COMPARING METHODS BY GROWTH RATE. Seconds depend on the machine, so we ask: if the input gets 10 times bigger, how much more work happens? Input size is n. For n = 1,000,000: logarithmic (log n) is about 20 steps; linear (n) is 1,000,000; linearithmic (n log n) is about 20,000,000; quadratic (n squared) is 1,000,000,000,000. Big-O is the notation: "binary search is O(log n)" means its work grows like log n. Quadratic work grows 100x when the input grows 10x.

COUNTERINTUITIVE: A BETTER ALGORITHM BEATS A FASTER COMPUTER. Sort 1 million items. Method X takes about n squared = 10^12 steps. Method Y takes about n log n = 2 x 10^7 steps. Run X on a computer 1,000 times faster: effective cost 10^9 steps. Run Y on the slow computer: 2 x 10^7. The slow computer with the better method wins by about 50x. Hardware cannot fix a bad growth rate.

TEMPTING BUT WRONG: "just time both programs and pick the faster one". Small tests lie. At n = 100 a quadratic method (10,000 steps) can beat a clever method with heavy setup work; at n = 1 million the order flips. Growth rate tells you what happens at sizes you have not tested.

WHAT THE DOMAIN COVERS (map): Searching (find one item: binary search). Sorting (put items in order: merge sort, quicksort). Graphs (things and connections: shortest route, who-knows-whom). Design strategies (reusable approaches: divide-and-conquer, greedy, dynamic programming). Limits (what cannot be solved fast: hard problems). Search and sort are the classic foundational examples, but they are not the whole domain: shortest path, minimum spanning tree, scheduling and knapsack are neither search nor sort. A fairer one-line statement: algorithms are about computing a correct answer efficiently, and the design strategies are what let one idea solve thousands of different problems. Sorting also exists largely to make searching cheap (sort once, then binary search many times).

CONNECTION TO DATA STRUCTURES. The two are one skill. Binary search works only because the list is sorted AND an array lets you jump to the middle in one step. On a linked list, reaching the middle takes n/2 steps, so binary search loses its advantage. Data structures are the containers; algorithms are what you do with them. Every cost is stated in Big-O (computer-science/complexity/big-o).

WHERE IT WINS IN PRACTICE. Geospatial: nearest hospital or shortest road route are graph and search problems; a naive nearest-neighbour check over 10 million map points is slow, a spatial index makes it fast. Data science: training repeats the same calculation millions of times, so a 2x better method saves days. GPUs: thousands of small tasks run at once, so which algorithms split into independent pieces decides what a GPU can speed up. Engineering and interviews: judging whether something still works at 100x the data.
payload.notes: Session opened with a request for a higher-level overview of Algorithms, to be followed by design strategies. Two diagnostic check-in questions (unscored, so not logged as a quiz): (1) binary search on 2 billion items: Craig said 31 steps because steps grow logarithmically with item count - correct. (2) n squared work with input 10x bigger: Craig said 100x more work - correct. Craig then proposed that algorithms exist to solve two fundamental problems, search and sort, and asked if that is fair. Answer given: partly fair (they are the classic foundational examples, and sorting mostly serves searching), but the domain is broader - graph problems (shortest path, spanning trees), optimization (knapsack, scheduling) and design strategies are neither. Craig chose to go next into design strategies (divide-and-conquer, greedy, dynamic programming), so the next session should teach those. payload.content:
TYPES OF PROBLEMS: the problem space of algorithms. Follow-up to the domain overview (event 108).

THE QUESTION. Craig asked: if design strategies let one idea solve thousands of problems, how many TYPES of problem are there? Surely not thousands. Answer: correct. There are two different things that were being mixed together.
- A PROBLEM TYPE is the question you are asked: "find this item", "put these in order", "what is the cheapest route".
- A DESIGN STRATEGY is the tool used to build the method: divide-and-conquer, greedy, dynamic programming.
Problem types are few. Real-world applications are thousands, but each one is a classic problem in disguise. The main skill is recognising which family a new problem belongs to. There is no official count; textbooks group them differently, usually into somewhere around 7 to 10 families.

CORRECTION TO THE EARLIER MAP. The map in the overview listed Searching, Sorting, Graphs, Design strategies and Limits as five rows of one list. That list mixed two different things. Searching, sorting and graphs are problem types (the question). Design strategies are the tools. Limits is a label that cuts across problem types. They are different axes and should not sit in one list.

THE FAMILIES (the question each one asks, a concrete case, and where it shows up):
1. SEARCHING. Is this item here, and where? Example: one name among 1 billion sorted names takes about 30 steps with binary search against up to 1,000,000,000 by scanning. Shows up in: dictionary lookups, finding a record, checking whether a username is taken.
2. SORTING AND ORDERING. Arrange items by a key. Example: 1 million items cost about 2 x 10^7 steps with n log n methods against 10^12 with n squared methods. Sorting also helps other problems: sort once and then binary search many times, spot duplicates (they end up next to each other), rank by score.
3. GRAPH PROBLEMS. Things and the connections between them: people and friendships, cities and roads, tasks and prerequisites. Four questions come up again and again. (a) Reachability: can I get from A to B at all? (traversal, BFS and DFS). (b) Shortest path: what is the cheapest route? (Dijkstra). (c) Spanning tree: what is the cheapest way to connect every point? (Prim, Kruskal). (d) Ordering with dependencies: which task goes first when some tasks need others done first? (topological sort). Example: a route app asking for the quickest way to the nearest hospital is a shortest-path problem.
4. OPTIMIZATION UNDER A LIMIT. Pick the best choice out of a huge number of possible choices, subject to a limit. Examples: knapsack (items with weights and values, a bag with a weight limit, maximise the value carried); interval scheduling (fit the most meetings into one room); making change. Making change for 30 with coins of 1, 15 and 25: the best answer is 15 + 15, which is 2 coins. Always grabbing the biggest coin first gives 25 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1, which is 6 coins.
5. STRING AND SEQUENCE PROBLEMS. Compare, match or compress text and other sequences. Examples: edit distance (the fewest single-character changes to turn one word into another, behind spell-checkers) and longest common subsequence (behind diff tools that show what changed between two files).
6. GEOMETRIC AND SPATIAL PROBLEMS. Questions about points and shapes in space. Example: the nearest neighbour of a point among 10 million map points. A naive check compares against all 10 million. A spatial index avoids that. This family is Craig's geospatial home ground.
7. NUMERIC PROBLEMS. Arithmetic and linear algebra at scale: multiplying very large numbers, solving systems of equations, multiplying matrices. Matrix multiplication is the core calculation repeated in neural-network training, which is why its speed matters so much.
8. HARD PROBLEMS (a label, not a separate family). Problems in any family where no fast method is known. Example: the travelling salesperson problem, visiting every city once and returning with the shortest total distance. 20 cities can be visited in 20! = about 2.4 x 10^18 different orders. At 1 billion orders checked per second, that is about 77 years. Checking every possibility is hopeless, so these problems need different thinking: settle for a good-enough answer or exploit extra structure. (NP-hardness is the formal name; it is a forward pointer, not taught yet.)

TWO AXES, ONE TABLE. The same few strategies cross many families, and one family can be attacked by several strategies. Typical pairings that appear in this book:
  Problem type (the question)        Typical strategy (the tool)
  Sorting                            divide-and-conquer (merge sort, quicksort)
  Shortest path, costs not negative  greedy (Dijkstra)
  Minimum spanning tree              greedy (Prim, Kruskal)
  Interval scheduling                greedy
  Knapsack                           dynamic programming
  Edit distance                      dynamic programming
Same problem, two strategies: making change for 30 with coins 1, 15, 25 is solved wrongly by greedy (6 coins) and correctly by dynamic programming (2 coins). That is why picking the strategy is a separate skill from recognising the problem.

THE TEMPTING BUT WRONG IDEA. "Algorithms is a list of thousands of separate problems, each needing its own trick." The reality is a handful of families and a handful of strategies. A new problem is usually a known one wearing different clothes: choosing which courses to take in what order is topological sort; a spell-checker is edit distance; the cheapest wiring for a village is a spanning tree.

REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS DISGUISED AS CLASSIC PROBLEMS: nearest hospital = shortest path; friend suggestions = graph traversal; spell-checker = edit distance; ordering university courses by prerequisites = topological sort; packing a van for the most valuable deliveries under a weight limit = knapsack.
payload.notes: Craig challenged the earlier claim that strategies solve 'thousands of problems': the problem space must be much smaller, so what are the most frequent TYPES of problem? He asked for a 'Types of Problems' section on the Algorithms page. His objection exposed a real flaw in the earlier map, which mixed problem types (searching, sorting, graphs) with a strategy row (design) and a limits label in one list. Corrected in this lesson by separating the two axes (problem type vs design strategy). The family list is a teaching grouping, not an official standard; flagged as such in the content. Check-in question to ask next (not yet answered, so nothing is scored): a delivery app must choose which of 40 orders fit in a van with a 100 kg limit to earn the most. Which family is that, and which strategy would NOT be trusted to solve it? Expected: optimization under a limit (knapsack), dynamic programming rather than greedy. Craig wants to go on to design strategies next; recursion is the prerequisite. Forward pointers already registered: NP-hardness, parallel algorithms on GPUs, spatial indexes.

questions.question: Your team's nightly test run calls a real weather service. About 1 run in 10 fails because the service is slow or down, even though your code is fine. A teammate says 'just retry failed tests 3 times'. Another says 'replace the weather call with a fake response in the tests'. What does each fix gain, what does each risk, and which would you choose for the pipeline that blocks merging?
questions.answer: Retries keep a real check that the integration is current but only prove it works most of the time; useful in long E2E chains. Mocks are fast but only show the API worked as once documented, so drift goes unseen. Chose mocking for the merge-blocking pipeline because a failure from network trouble is costly and unrelated to the code.
questions.feedback: Correct. A merge gate should fail only when the developer's own code is wrong, so a flaky third-party call does not belong in it. Mocking removes the dependency rather than ignoring the failure. The drift risk Craig named is covered by a separate check that cannot block merges, such as a nightly run against the real service or a contract test that confirms the real API still returns the shape the mock assumes.

questions.question: A teammate says 'our unit tests are at 95% code coverage, so we're safe to ship'. Give one concrete way a codebase could have 95% coverage and still contain a serious bug. Then say what coverage actually tells you, and what it does not.
questions.answer: 95% coverage is not 95% reliability. The 5% untested could be the login code, hiding a serious bug. Coverage says most code has been tested, not whether the most critical code has.
questions.feedback: Good point that coverage does not weight code by importance, so an untested login path can hide a serious bug. The misconception is the phrase 'has been tested'. Coverage only measures which lines were executed while the tests ran. It does not measure whether any test checked the result. Example: a function add_discount(price, items) returns price * 0.9 when it should return price * 0.1. A test calls add_discount(100, 5) and asserts nothing. Every line runs, so that function shows 100% coverage, yet the bug passes. Coverage can show code that is definitely unchecked (the 5% never run), but it cannot show that the other 95% is checked correctly.

gaps.text: Treated code coverage as meaning the covered code 'has been tested'. Coverage only measures lines executed, not whether tests assert correct results, so 100% coverage can coexist with wrong behaviour.

payload.content:
RECOGNISING A PROBLEM: how to tell which family a new problem belongs to. Extends the Types of Problems lesson (event 109).

THE RULE: LOOK AT THE SHAPE OF THE ANSWER, NOT THE SETTING. A map app, a bank and a game all contain the same few problems; only the story changes. Ask: what does the finished answer look like?

THE CLUE TABLE (answer shape -> family -> example):
- Yes/no, or a position in a list -> Searching -> is this username taken?
- The same items in a new order -> Sorting -> rank 1 million products by rating
- A route from A to B -> Graph: shortest path -> fastest drive to a hospital
- A set of links that joins everything -> Graph: spanning tree -> least cable to join 12 villages
- A to-do order where "X comes before Y" -> Graph: dependency ordering (topological sort) -> compile 200 files, some needing others first
- Pairs, one from each of two groups -> Matching (technically a graph problem; the clue is different enough to name separately) -> 50 drivers paired with 50 riders
- A chosen subset that fits a limit -> Optimization under a limit -> which orders fit a 100 kg van
- Groups of similar things, with nobody giving the groups in advance -> Clustering -> split 1 million customers into segments by spending
- A number for how different two texts are, or the changed lines -> String and sequence -> spell-checker, diff
- Closest, inside or overlapping, in space -> Geometry -> nearest of 10 million map points
- Numbers that solve equations or fit a curve -> Numeric -> multiply two matrices
- Best settings for knobs that slide smoothly -> Continuous optimization -> train a neural network

NEW FAMILY LINES ADDED TO THE EARLIER LIST: matching, clustering, continuous optimization. CONTINUOUS means each knob can sit at any value in a range, like a volume dial. Knapsack is the opposite kind (discrete): you pick items from a list, like ordering from a menu. The tools differ: training a network follows the slope of the error downhill, which is the engine behind deep learning (5 million knobs adjusted so the error falls).

THE WEIGHT ON AN EDGE DOES NOT DECIDE THE FAMILY. Cost, distance and time are just numbers on the links. The same flight network can be asked three different questions, and the shape of the answer separates them:
- PATH: one route from A to B. Cheapest way to fly Pune to Berlin with stopovers allowed, each flight having a price. Shortest path.
- NETWORK (spanning tree): a web of links that joins everything, branching allowed. Connect 12 cities with the least total flight distance so any city can reach any other. Minimum spanning tree.
- TOUR: one closed loop through every stop, returning to the start. A courier starts at the depot (the home base, such as a warehouse), visits 25 stops once each and returns to the depot with the least distance. Travelling salesperson problem: the hard label.
Cost or distance can be the weight in any of the three. What differs is the shape.

WORKED EXAMPLE, TREE VERSUS TOUR. Depot in the centre, four stops 10 km away to the north, east, south and west. Spanning tree: four spokes, 4 x 10 = 40 km. A courier cannot branch (one person is in one place), so the tour goes depot -> N -> E -> S -> W -> depot: 10 + 14.14 + 14.14 + 14.14 + 10 = about 62.4 km (the corner-to-corner hops are 10 x root 2 = 14.14 km). The tree is cheaper because it can branch. Another order, N -> S -> E -> W, is worse: about 74.1 km. The tree is always a floor under the tour (drop one hop from a tour and what is left is a spanning tree). So a tour is not a spanning tree, even though both visit every point. Shortest path asks about two named end points; the tour asks about every stop.

TRAVEL TIME. When road weights are times, time = length / average speed, never length x speed. A 10 km road at 50 km/h takes 10 / 50 = 0.2 hours = 12 minutes. Multiplying gives 500, which means nothing. With time as the weight, the shortest path is the fastest route.

DEPENDENCIES ARE A WEB OF ARROWS, NOT A TREE. In a tree each item hangs from exactly one parent. A file can need two other files, so a dependency graph is a web of arrows. If A needs B and B needs A, no valid order exists.

THREE TRAPS.
1. Real tasks chain several problems. "Show the 3 nearest open pharmacies by drive time" is: filter for open (a simple search on an attribute), then a spatial search for nearby candidates among 10 million points (geometry), then shortest path for the drive time to each, then sort. Close in a straight line is not close by road: a pharmacy 1 km away across a river may be 25 minutes by road. So take about 10 nearby candidates, compute drive times for all, and keep the best 3. Second chain: "choose the fewest cell towers so all 200 villages are within range of one" is a geometry step (work out which villages each candidate site covers) followed by choosing a subset of towers. The subset step carries the hard label: with 1,000 candidate sites there are 2^1000 (about 1.07 x 10^301) subsets, so checking all is impossible, and in practice you settle for a good-enough answer (for example keep adding the tower that covers the most uncovered villages). Name each step before choosing any method.
2. Looks hard, isn't. Pairing 50 drivers with 50 riders has 50! (about 3 x 10^64) possible pairings, so brute force is hopeless. But matching is a solved family with a fast method needing roughly 50^3 = 125,000 steps. The number of possibilities does not tell you the problem is hard. (At 8 vans and 8 zones there are only 8! = 40,320 assignments, which a computer checks instantly; the fast method matters as the size grows.)
3. Looks easy, isn't. Visiting 25 stops and returning with the least distance feels like shortest path but is the travelling salesperson problem, the hard label. Check: does the question name a start and an end (path), or say visit everything and return (tour)?

SEARCH DETAIL. 500,000 company names sorted by name need at most 19 steps by binary search (2^19 = 524,288, which is at least 500,000). A binary search tree gives about 19 steps only if it is balanced. A tree built by inserting names that are already in sorted order becomes a single chain, and a lookup can take up to 500,000 steps. A sorted array can be binary searched directly.

STRING DETAIL. Showing which lines changed between two versions of a 2,000-line config file is the longest-common-subsequence problem (the family behind diff tools).

NUMERIC DETAIL. Multiplying two 4,096 x 4,096 tables of numbers takes 4,096^3, about 69 billion, multiplications by the plain method. This is the numeric family and the core calculation of neural-network training.

TEMPTING BUT WRONG FOR KNAPSACK: PICK BY VALUE PER KG. A rider can carry 10 kg. Order A weighs 2 kg and tips 12 (6 per kg). Order B weighs 4 kg and tips 20 (5 per kg). Order C weighs 6 kg and tips 24 (4 per kg). Taking the best tip per kg first, with no going back: A (2 kg) then B (4 kg) makes 6 kg and 32 in tips; C no longer fits (6 + 6 = 12 kg). The best choice is B + C = 10 kg and 44 in tips. So the per-kg rule gets 32 against the best 44. This is the same instance as the van with a 50 kg limit scaled down (A 10 kg for 60, B 20 kg for 100, C 30 kg for 120: ratio rule 160, best 220). The family is optimization under a limit (knapsack); greedy by ratio is the strategy not to trust; dynamic programming is the one to use.

payload.content:
FOLLOW-UP ON PROBLEM TYPES: what a spanning tree looks like, the knapsack goal versus method, and what to do with a hard problem (cell towers).

WHAT A SPANNING TREE LOOKS LIKE. A spanning tree is a set of links that connects every point, with no loops. Example: five villages A to E and five possible roads, with lengths in km: A-B 4, A-C 3, B-C 2, B-D 5, D-E 4. Building every road costs 4 + 3 + 2 + 5 + 4 = 18 km.
ASCII map of the possible roads:
 A ---4--- B
  \       / \
   3     2   5
    \   /     \
      C        D ---4--- E
The roads A-B, B-C and A-C form a loop. A tree has no loop, so one road of the loop must go. Dropping A-B (4 km) leaves A-C 3, B-C 2, B-D 5, D-E 4 = 14 km. Dropping A-C leaves 15 km. Dropping B-C leaves 16 km. So this map has exactly three spanning trees, costing 14, 15 and 16 km, and the cheapest one is the minimum spanning tree. ASCII picture of the cheapest tree (14 km):
 A         B
  \       / \
   3     2   5
    \   /     \
      C        D ---4--- E
Facts: 5 villages always need exactly 4 links (n villages need n - 1 links); every village can reach every other along the links; there are no loops; the links may branch (C has two links and B has two).

KNAPSACK: THE GOAL VERSUS THE METHOD. The goal is the most tips earned while staying within the 10 kg limit. For orders A (2 kg, tip 12), B (4 kg, tip 20) and C (6 kg, tip 24) that goal gives 44 (B + C, exactly 10 kg). A method is a way of reaching the goal. Trying every set of orders always works: 3 orders give 8 sets, 30 orders give 2^30 = 1,073,741,824 sets, so it stops being practical. The shortcut of taking the best tip per kg first and never going back is a method, and it is wrong here (it gets 32). Dynamic programming reaches the true best without trying every set; it is taught later.

HARD PROBLEMS: IS THERE A RIGHT ANSWER, AND IS THERE A METHOD? Take the cell-tower problem: choose the fewest towers so every one of 200 villages is within range of at least one (the formal name is set cover). Yes, there is a right answer: some smallest number of towers exists and a best set achieves it. 'Hard' does not mean no answer. It means no method is known that is both always right and fast on every input. The options:
1. Try every set of towers. Always right, hopeless in time: 1,000 candidate sites give 2^1000 (about 1.07 x 10^301) sets.
2. Greedy: repeatedly add the tower that covers the most still-uncovered villages. Fast, but not always best. Small case with 6 villages: tower T1 covers villages {1, 2, 3, 4}, T2 covers {1, 3, 5}, T3 covers {2, 4, 6}. Greedy takes T1 first (it covers 4), then needs T2 for village 5 and T3 for village 6, so 3 towers. The best is T2 + T3, which covers all six with 2 towers. A known result: greedy is never worse than about ln(n) + 1 times the best, which for 200 villages is ln(200) + 1, about 6.3 times. In practice it is usually much closer.
3. Exact solvers for real instances. 'Hard' describes the worst case. Many real instances of a few hundred villages can be solved exactly, with a proof that the answer is best, by integer-programming or branch-and-bound solvers, even though the worst case is exponential.
4. Use the problem's structure. Tower range is a circle on a map, and that geometry can allow better methods than the general case.
Same pattern as making change for 30 with coins 1, 15 and 25: greedy gives 6 coins, best is 2. A hard problem is where you accept 'good enough, with a known worst case' or 'exact, but only for the sizes a solver can handle'.

questions.question: Three engineers get the same road map of 40 towns, with the distance of every road. Engineer A is asked: what is the shortest drive from town 1 to town 40? Engineer B is asked: what is the least total length of road that must exist so every town can reach every other? Engineer C is asked: start in town 1, visit every other town once, and return to town 1 with the least total driving. (1) Name the family of each request. (2) Say which one carries the hard label. (3) Give the one clue in the wording that tells A, B and C apart.

questions.feedback: Right on parts 1 and 2. Part 3 was not answered, so here is the clue. The wording tells you the shape of the answer. A names two end points, 'from town 1 to town 40', so the answer is a single path. B says 'every town can reach every other' and asks for the least road that must exist. Nobody drives it, and it may branch, so the answer is a network: a spanning tree. C says 'visit every other town once and return', so the answer is one closed loop through every stop, a tour. The tour is the hard one: the other 39 towns can be visited in 39! (about 2 x 10^46) orders. At 1 billion orders checked per second that is about 6.5 x 10^29 years, so checking them all is impossible. Cost, distance and time can be the weight in all three; the wording that differs is whether it names two end points, asks for everything to be connected, or asks for a loop through everything.

questions.question: In your own words, what does binary search do, and what must be true about the data before you can use it?
questions.answer: Halves the search range at every step. The data must be sorted (ascending or descending). Compare the target with the midpoint, throw away the half that cannot contain it, and repeat until the value is found.
questions.feedback: Right: sorted data is what lets one comparison with the middle rule out half the range. It can be written as a loop or as recursion. The answer left out the stopping rule: stop when the value is found or when the remaining range is empty.

questions.question: You have 1,000,000 sorted numbers stored as a linked list instead of an array. Would binary search still take about 20 steps? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. Reaching the middle of a linked list takes n/2 = 500,000 steps, then about 250,000 for the next middle, and so on, so the total is up to about 1,000,000 steps in the worst case.
questions.feedback: Right. The walking costs 500,000 + 250,000 + 125,000 + ... which adds up to about 1,000,000, the same as scanning from the start. Binary search still makes only about 20 comparisons, but the walking between them costs almost everything. That is why it needs an array, where jumping to the middle takes one step.

questions.question: On a sorted array of 1,000,000 numbers, you search for a value that is not in it. About how many steps before binary search can say it is not there, and how does it know to stop?
questions.answer: About 20 steps. 1,000,000 to about 1,000 is roughly 10 halvings and 1,000 to 1 is roughly 10 more. When the last remaining number is not equal to the target, it stops.
questions.feedback: Right: 2^20 is about 1,048,576, so a million items need at most about 20 halvings, and a miss costs the same as the worst case for a hit. Precisely, the search stops when the remaining range becomes empty, after the last single item is checked and does not match.
